background: A study wants to find out why food-bank sites run out of stock. Before committing, it tested three **directions** on invented food-bank networks whose cause is known: **mining records** the sites already keep, **asking people** who run them, and **simulating** how stock moves. Each direction has approaches of its own, nine in all. The example is fictional, made to show how a choice among research directions reads as a report.

Each approach was tried three times on five invented networks, each with one planted cause, and a run succeeded when it named that cause. One records approach was run twice as identical copies, so the gap between the copies shows how far chance alone moves a result.
story.intent: The research lead asked: “To find why food-bank sites run out of stock, should the study mine records, ask people, or simulate, and which approach should it use?”
questions: Which direction finds the planted cause most often, pooled over its approaches?
Does that direction work on every kind of cause, including those nobody records?
Within the leading direction, is one approach ahead by more than chance?
story.rule: Fixed before the runs: carry forward the direction that recovers the planted cause most often, if it reaches 60% of valid runs and does not fall below 50% on any of the five networks. Within it, choose the leading approach only if it leads the next by more than the two identical copies differ; otherwise carry the whole direction forward.

alternatives.a1: Regression on inventory logs (mining records): a statistical model of stock levels from the sites' own logs. Its identical copy is a1r.
alternatives.a1r: The same regression on inventory logs, run again as an identical copy, to show how much chance alone moves a result.
alternatives.a2: Seasonal time series (mining records): looks for repeating patterns in stock levels over the year.
alternatives.a3: Text mining of case reports (mining records): reads the sites' written incident reports for causes.
alternatives.b1: Short survey of coordinators (asking people): a brief written questionnaire for site coordinators.
alternatives.b2: Structured interviews (asking people): set questions asked in conversation with coordinators and volunteers.
alternatives.b3: Open interviews (asking people): free conversation with coordinators and volunteers.
alternatives.c1: Agent-based simulation (simulating): models each donor, volunteer and visitor and lets stock-outs emerge.
alternatives.c2: Queueing model (simulating): models stock as queues of arrivals and departures.

cases.k1: Seasonal demand swings: demand peaks every winter. A cause the records show clearly.
cases.k2: Supplier reliability: one supplier delivers late. A cause the records show.
cases.k3: Donation timing: drop-offs bunch at the start of the week. A cause records and models can both show.
cases.k4: Volunteer turnover: the weekend crew keeps changing and nobody records who works, so only people can tell.
cases.k5: Storage capacity: the cold room is too small and its use is not logged, so only people or a model can tell.

story.covers: Whether each approach named the planted cause, how good its evidence was judged on a 10-point scale, and how confident it said it was, three runs on each of five invented networks.
story.notCovered: Real food banks, the cost and time of each approach beyond the per-run cost listed, and causes that combine. Nine runs failed to finish and are left out.

glossary.meaning: The run named the cause built into that invented network.
Counted over every approach in a direction together.

decision.headline: Carry **Ask people** forward and use **structured interviews** within it.
detail: Asking people recovered the planted cause in 32 of 44 valid runs (73%), mining records in 23 of 44 (52%) and simulating in 9 of 26 (35%). No concept fell below 56% for asking people.

Within it, structured interviews recovered the cause in 13 of 15 runs (87%) against 10 of 14 (71%) for open interviews, a lead of 15 points. The two identical copies of one records approach differed by 7 points (9 and 8 of 15), so the lead is more than twice the noise.

checks.label: Pooled recovery of the leading direction at least 60% of valid runs
No concept below 50% for that direction
Leading approach ahead of the next by more than the identical copies differ

conditions: Five invented food-bank concepts, each with one planted cause
Three runs per approach and concept
The rule rests on recovering the planted cause; evidence quality and stated confidence did not enter it
limits: The interval for structured interviews (about 62% to 96%) overlaps the one for open interviews (about 45% to 88%): the rule is met, the approach is not settled.
Mining records did better where records exist: 20 of 26 runs (77%) on the three concepts that have them, against 18 of 27 (67%) for asking people. Three concepts show a pattern, not a tested rule.
The three records approaches stated High confidence in 15 of their 21 failed runs and in 16 of their 23 successful ones, so their stated confidence says little about whether they are right.
The queueing model was not run on seasonal demand because it has no demand input, and three runs ended without a conclusion; they are counted as invalid, not as failures.
changes: A decision to study only networks that keep detailed records would put mining records first
More concepts, which would narrow the intervals the choice of approach rests on

readings.compared: Nine approaches in three directions; the two copies of the regression on inventory logs are identical, so their difference is chance alone.
readings.results: Structured interviews recovered the planted cause most often, 13 of 15 runs (87%), and open interviews 10 of 14 (71%); the records approaches recovered it in 43% to 60% of runs and the simulations in 27% to 40%. Evidence quality was similar except for the simulations, rated lower.
readings.differences: Against the regression on inventory logs, no approach's recovery differs by more than chance; structured interviews come closest (+27 points, interval −5 to +53). The simulations' evidence quality is lower by about 1.4 to 1.7 points of 10, intervals below zero. The identical copy differs from the original by 7 points, the size of chance here.
readings.groups: Pooled by direction, asking people recovered the cause in 32 of 44 valid runs (73%), mining records in 23 of 44 (52%) and simulating in 9 of 26 (35%).
readings.cases: The directions split by kind of cause. Mining records did well where records exist (seasonal demand, supplier, donation timing) and poorly on volunteer turnover and storage, which nobody logs; asking people never fell below 5 of 9 on any network.
readings.observations: 396 observations: three measures for each run. Nine are invalid because their runs did not finish.
